subject: Tokenized load landscape and graceful fallbacks — methodology & evidence

Subject: RFP follow-up: exact runtime tests and tokenization assumptions

Kimberly —

Thanks for the RFP response packet. Before we map your results onto our acceptance criteria we need a few precise clarifications about the test harness and tokenization assumptions used in your latency/throughput numbers. Can you confirm the following pieces of information?

1) Tokenization: did you tokenize on the client or server side for the throughput runs? Were multi-byte characters or long whitespace sequences normalized?
2) Request mix: the PDF shows "median request length 48 tokens" — can you provide the exact percentile breakdown (P50/P90/P95/P99) and the distribution used to seed the synthetic generator?
3) KV/prefix cache: when you report tail latency under burst, is prefix KV cache warm, partially warm, or cold? How many replica shards were in the test cluster?
4) Warmup policy and duration for each endpoint variant.

We'd like short answers with data pointers — CSVs or quick artifacts are fine. Our acceptance window is narrow; aim to get this back by EOD PT today.

— Alice
Alice Jones
Senior SWE, Performance Engineering
Globex Corporation

From: Kimberly Park <kimberly_park@redwood.ai>

Subject: Re: RFP follow-up: exact runtime tests and tokenization assumptions

Alice —

Thanks for the specific asks. Below is a concise mapping back to each numbered point; I've attached the CSV export of the synthetic seed distribution and the playbook we used to run the lab. Key highlights up front: all numbers in the public RFP packet reflect server-side tokenization (BPE, UTF-8 normalization); our burst tests used a partially warmed prefix/KV cache (see details). Attachments: redwood-load-playbook.csv, kv-prefix-evidence.pdf.

1) Tokenization
- Per-test: tokenization was executed server-side in the serving runtime to ensure consistent tokenizer versions across clients.
- Normalization: we apply NFC unicode normalization and collapse runs of >8 whitespace characters to a single token boundary in the synthetic generator to mirror real user inputs.
- Edge cases: multi-byte emoji sequences are preserved and counted as multiple BPE tokens; we include a small tail of long whitespace messages in the seed set (0.6% of requests).

2) Request mix (attached CSV: redwood-load-playbook.csv)
- Percentiles measured from the production-like corpus used to generate synthetic traffic: P50=46 tokens, P90=98 tokens, P95=130 tokens, P99=212 tokens.
- Generator: mixture model with three modes — short chat (0–64 tokens, 73% weight), medium form-fills (65–160 tokens, 22% weight), long completions (161+ tokens, 5% weight). Seed CSV contains per-mode histograms and RNG seeds.

3) KV/prefix cache state and replica topology
- Burst runs: the reported tail-latency envelopes used a partially warmed KV/prefix cache where 78% of requests hit an active KV entry (simulating typical session reuse). Cold-start profiles are provided separately in the attached kv-prefix-evidence.pdf.
- Replica set: production-grade test cluster had 4 serving replicas per model variant with multi-replica fanout disabled for the baseline figures (single-replica routing). During a high-availability sweep we retried with 8 replicas to validate saturation characteristics; results are annotated in the CSV.

4) Warmup policy and durations
- Endpoint warmup: A staged warmup — 5 minutes at 10% traffic, then 10 minutes at 50% traffic, then full load. Warmup durations are encoded in the playbook and applied per-model-shape to prime kernels and allocator pools.

Quick notes on methodology hygiene:
- All benchmark traces include per-token timestamps (host-time and kernel execution time), which are available on request as gzipped traces for P95/P99 tail decomposition.
- We run each scenario 3× with fresh VM instances to capture variance and include the median run for public results.

Next steps: If you want the cold-cache re-run with identical replica topology we can schedule a 2-hour lab window tomorrow morning PT.

Regards,
Kimberly Park
Director, Product Operations (Performance)
Redwood Inference

Attachments: redwood-load-playbook.csv (CSV, 24KB), kv-prefix-evidence.pdf (PDF, 1.1MB)

Thanks, Kimberly. Couple of follow-ups after skimming the CSV:

- Can you confirm which tokenizer binary and version was used (we need exact git tag or pip wheel hash for compliance)?
- For the partially warmed cache profile: what was the TTL/eviction policy used to generate the 78% hit rate? Does the KV TTL align with session cookie lifetimes?
- Regarding the per-token timestamps: can you share one gzipped trace for the P99 window we can ingest into our trace parser?

Also, for acceptance criteria, our security/compliance team wants a short description of how you isolate customer traffic in Dedicated mode during these runs (brief topology diagram would be ideal). Is that safe to include in the Appendix PDF?

We need these items within 6 hours to make the internal scoring meeting.

— Perf Team
